title: investor view negative power prices expose market opportunity  reeii 2026 07 27
author: Domenico Tripodi
text:
July 27 - As renewable energy capacity grows across U.S. and Europe, increasing prevalence of negative power prices creates challenges and opportunities for infrastructure investors.
Germany recorded 573 hours of negative wholesale electricity prices in 2025, up from 457 hours in 2024. Spain, Sweden, the Netherlands and France also passed 500 ​negative-price hours by the end of October 2025, while Finland and Denmark's price zones exceeded 400. In the U.S. state of California, below zero power prices ‌in the southern SP15 hub more than doubled in 2024 and curtailments rose. In ERCOT, which manages around 90% of Texas electricity load, day-ahead prices dropped nearly 50% in 2024 as almost 10 GW of new solar and storage entered the market.
The interpretation that renewable energy growth is crashing the market misses the point entirely.
Negative power prices are a result of marginal cost pricing based on an outdated model designed for fossil fuel ​generation, not a symptom of a failing renewable energy market.
The system is increasingly dominated by technologies with zero or near-zero marginal costs such as wind, solar and batteries, and ​the market architecture has not caught up, yet.
Current regulatory debates risk compounding the problem; for example, proposals to strip emissions trading system (ETS) carbon ⁠price signals from electricity price formation would reduce a wholesale price floor that uncontracted renewable assets still depend on for revenue.
This mismatch between technologies and market design has consequences for the ​financing and contracting of power assets.
Grid constraints compound the issue. In many markets, transmission capacity has not kept pace with the deployment of new power generation, creating congestion that further widens the ​gap between headline prices and the revenues assets actually capture.

A significant number of renewable energy assets in operation today were built and financed when headline power prices were higher, the upside for merchant power sales looked stronger and capital was cheaper. Those assumptions no longer hold.
In a structurally lower-price environment where volatile prices can jump above and below zero, it is no longer enough for an asset simply to produce renewable electricity. Assets ​must be able to monetise power effectively across increasingly volatile and constrained markets.
Revenue quality has overtaken production volume as the most important variable. Key drivers include capturing price, zonal and congestion ​exposure, curtailment, balancing strategy, offtake quality and financing the resilience of the power grid. Policy tools have only partially helped, for example Contracts for Difference (CfDs) that have brought welcome revenue stability do not fully incentivise ‌flexibility, energy storage ⁠or system integration, all key priorities for grid operators.
Investors must prepare for structural change. Electricity markets are transitioning towards a different pricing and revenue model, one that rewards capacity, flexibility and reliability, not just energy production. The commercial model for infrastructure investment must evolve with them.

Assets and portfolios designed for the old model will continue to face pressure. Those designed for the new one, combining generation with storage, pairing production with flexible offtake, integrating across technologies and locations, will capture the next phase of value.
Pricing pressure, reduced liquidity and valuation resets have opened a gap between ​where assets trade and where long-term fundamentals point. ​That creates a specific and arguably time-limited ⁠opportunity for more investors willing to look beyond headline prices.
This is particularly true in markets that experience the most severe consequences of these structural imbalances. For example, Nordic operational onshore wind assets are trading at valuations that reflect market dislocation rather than long-term fundamentals. Swedish onshore wind transaction ​volumes have fallen sharply since 2021, driven by price divergence between bidding zones and a general loss of market confidence.
But the medium-term ​outlook tells a different story: ⁠electricity demand is projected to grow significantly, driven by data centres, electrification and industrial expansion; zonal price spreads are expected to narrow as grid infrastructure improves and expands, and reduced greenfield development is lowering future price cannibalisation risk. Solar and wind growth has slowed in the EU and in Sweden only one small wind turbine order was placed in the first nine months of 2025.
For investors able ⁠to acquire operational ​portfolios at attractive entry prices and then improve how that power is contracted, balanced, and financed, the value case ​can be compelling.
This is not a passive strategy and requires patience. It involves forming an independent view of where system value is heading and being willing to invest when others are retreating, provided the fundamentals support it. And it ​demands the discipline to structure assets and portfolios for a market that may take several years to fully rebalance. For investors prepared to do the work, that is where the opportunity lies.
